title: An alarm you can't tap off: AlarmKit and Android exact alarms
excerpt: How Ryup's alarm rings from a locked phone with the app closed, using AlarmKit on iPhone and exact alarms on Android, plus bugs found only on real devices.
content:
An alarm clock has one job, and it is the one job nobody forgives you for missing. If a to-do app loses a task, you are annoyed. If an alarm app stays silent, you lose your morning.

Ryup is an alarm that you cannot tap off. To stop it, you read a short passage aloud and answer a question or two. That takes two or three minutes, and it is much harder to do half asleep than a single tap. There is no snooze button, on purpose.

That idea only works if the alarm rings every single time. This post is about how we made that true on both iPhone and Android, and what went wrong on the way.

## The problem: your phone wants to save battery, not wake you

Phones are very good at stopping apps that are not on screen. After a while, the operating system puts your app to sleep to save battery. A normal app cannot just say "ring at 6:30" and trust that it will still be awake at 6:30.

So the rule for a reliable alarm is simple: **do not ask the app to ring. Ask the phone to ring.** Both iPhone and Android have a built-in alarm system that keeps running when apps are closed, locked or killed. Our job is to hand the alarm over to that system.

## iPhone: AlarmKit

On iPhone we use **AlarmKit**, an Apple framework (a ready-made set of tools) that gives third-party apps the same alarm powers as the built-in Clock app. An AlarmKit alarm rings through **Silent mode** and through an active **Focus** (the "Do Not Disturb" family of modes). It survived force-quitting the app and rebooting the phone in our tests, on real hardware, not only in the simulator.

Three things surprised us:

- **It needs a recent iPhone.** AlarmKit arrived with iOS 26, and the cleanest way to build the alert is available from iOS 26.1. So Ryup requires iOS 26.1. That shrinks the audience a little, but for an alarm clock, honesty about ringing matters more than reach.
- **The system draws the alert, not us.** The lock screen moment is Apple's: a title, a Stop button and one optional extra button. Our Flutter screen is what you see after the app opens. We had to design around that.
- **It has its own permission,** separate from notifications.

We also chose what **not** to build. Older alarm apps keep themselves alive by playing silent audio in the background. It can drain the battery, it can break if you force-quit the app, and Apple has been rejecting new apps for it. We did not want to build a new product on a trick that App Review is actively refusing.

## Android: exact alarms, a loud screen and a sound service

On Android the building blocks are different, and there are more of them:

- An **exact alarm** is an alarm that fires at the exact minute, instead of "sometime around then". Android allows the special permission for it only to apps whose core purpose is an alarm clock or calendar. Ryup qualifies, and we declare it in Google Play.
- A **full-screen intent** lets the ringing alarm take over the lock screen. Google keeps this permission only for alarm and calling apps.
- A **foreground service** (a service Android promises not to kill, shown with a notification) keeps the alarm sound playing.
- We set Android 8.0 as the minimum, after finding that the alarm could not ring reliably on Android 7.

Google reviews each of these. Adding a new permission can add a new form to fill in, so we treat the permission list as part of every release.

## Knowing whether you woke up

Neither system can tell us whether you actually got up, so the phone checks for itself. If an alarm rang and nobody finished the activity in time, the phone's own alarm code books the next ring, on both platforms, without asking a server. Only the numbers (how long a ring lasts, how long to wait, how many tries) come from our backend, so we can tune them without an app update. We explain that retry ladder in detail in [why Ryup has no snooze button](/blog/why-ryup-has-no-snooze-backend-tuned-retry-ladder).

## The bugs tests did not catch

We have a large test suite, and it was green the whole time. Yet seven real bugs came out of the alarm layer and the app disagreeing about what state an alarm was in. Every one was found by **using the app on a real phone**, none by the tests.

That taught us two habits:

1. Write down who decides the alarm's state, and the rules that keep the app and the phone's alarm layer in agreement. Ours is a short list of nine rules, each next to the bug that created it.
2. Test the scenarios people actually live in: a locked phone, a force-quit app, a reboot in the middle of the night, a phone left in Silent mode.

One small example: for a while, the alarm rang into a dark screen and the app never said why. The alarm was fine, but nobody had told the user which permission was missing. A working alarm that looks broken is still a broken alarm.

## What we would tell another team

- Hand the alarm to the phone's own alarm system. Never ask your app to stay awake.
- Check what each store allows before you design around a permission.
- Keep the "did they wake up?" logic on a server, so both platforms behave the same.
- Test on real phones in the real situations, with the screen locked.

Ryup is live on Google Play, and the iPhone version is on its way. If you want the other half of the story, read how we structured the app in [our Flutter architecture post](/blog/flutter-app-architecture-riverpod-ios-android) and how the server decides a morning counted in [the Go backend post](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)
author: Softogram

title: One Flutter codebase, two platforms: how we structured Ryup
excerpt: The Flutter architecture behind Ryup: feature folders, Riverpod state, errors as values, build flavors and screenshot tests that caught real bugs.
content:
When we started Ryup, we made one rule that shaped everything after it: **iPhone and Android are equals from day one.** No "Android first, iPhone later". A feature counts as done only when it is right on both.

Flutter is what makes that practical. It lets one team write one codebase that runs on both. This post shows how we organised that codebase so it stays easy to change, and the habits that caught real bugs.

## Layers: each part has one job

Think of the app as four layers. Each layer only talks to the one below it.

1. **Screens and widgets** show things and send taps. They never make decisions. A screen does not decide "is this user over their plan limit?"
2. **Controllers** hold the state of a screen (what it is showing right now) and make the decisions. We use **Riverpod** for this. It is a state management library, which means it keeps the data a screen needs in one place and updates the screen when that data changes.
3. **Repositories** fetch and save data. They are the only part that knows where data comes from.
4. **Data sources** do the real work: network calls with Dio, a local database with Drift, and phone features such as notifications and permissions.

The payoff is practical. When a plan limit changes, you edit one controller, not twelve screens.

## One folder per feature

Inside the app, code is grouped by **feature**, not by type. There is a folder for alarms, one for auth, one for billing, one for home, and so on. Each feature has its own screens, controllers and data code.

When someone asks "where is the billing code?", the answer is one folder. A new developer can read a feature from top to bottom without jumping around the whole project.

## Errors are values, not surprises

A common beginner problem: a network call fails, an exception flies upward, and the screen shows a blank page or crashes.

We return a **result** instead. A result is either "ok, here is the value" or "failed, here is why". Repositories return results, and raw errors from the network or database never leak out of the data layer. The controller turns a failure into something a person can understand, in plain language.

Here is the idea in a few lines:

```dart
sealed class Result<T> {}
class Ok<T> extends Result<T> { final T value; Ok(this.value); }
class Err<T> extends Result<T> { final Failure failure; Err(this.failure); }
```

Because the failure is a normal value, the compiler reminds us to handle it. Every screen also has to define four states: loading, empty, error and normal. A screen with only the happy path does not ship.

## Platform differences live in one place

iPhone and Android genuinely differ in places: permissions, purchases, background work. The temptation is to scatter `if (Platform.isIOS)` checks across the app. We do not.

Instead, platform-specific code sits behind a small **service** with one interface. The check for "which phone is this?" happens once, in one factory function, and the rest of the app just calls the service. Permissions go through one central service too. For native Swift and Kotlin code we use Pigeon, which generates the bridge between Flutter and native code, instead of hand-written message passing that is easy to get subtly wrong.

We also use **build flavors**: separate dev, staging and production builds with different app IDs and settings, so a test build never touches real data.

## Matching the design exactly

Ryup's look is a sky that changes through the day. The background and colours move from deep night blues to sunrise coral. We took the exact values from the design prototype, and the app bundles its fonts locally, so the alarm screen needs no network at all. We even wrote down the rule: if the written design notes and the prototype disagree, the prototype wins.

## The tests that saw what other tests missed

Two visual bugs once shipped past all our normal tests. The night moon drew as a bare outline ring instead of a crescent, and the bottom tab bar had the wrong height. The tests were all checking text, and neither bug changed any text.

The fix was **golden tests**: tests that take a picture of a screen and compare it pixel by pixel with a saved reference. Because screens depend on the time of day, we pin the time in the test. A test whose result changes with the clock is not a real test. Pictures drawn on a Mac and on a Linux build machine differ slightly, so the same test runs in both.

## Battery, memory and size are features

For an alarm app, battery and install size matter. Our rules are short:

- No polling loops. The app never asks "did they wake up?" on a timer. The server tracks that.
- Every controller and subscription is closed when a screen goes away.
- Any new package that wraps native code gets its install-size cost checked before we add it.

## What we would tell another team

- Split screens, decisions, data and platform code into layers on day one.
- Return errors as values, and write the failure message for a human.
- Keep platform checks in one place.
- Add screenshot tests as soon as a screen looks right.

The whole app talks to a Go server, which we cover in [the backend post](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app). And the hardest single feature of the app, the alarm itself, is in [the alarm post](/blog/reliable-alarm-ios-alarmkit-android-exact-alarms).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)
author: Softogram

title: Ryup's Go backend: Gin, Postgres and an AI scorer
excerpt: How Ryup's Go backend works: Gin API, Postgres, voice clips, speech-to-text, AI scoring, scheduled jobs and a load limit that answers fast at 6 AM.
content:
A mobile app looks like it lives on the phone. For Ryup, the phone is only half of it. When you wake up and read a passage aloud, a server has to receive your voice, turn it into words, judge your answer, and remember that your morning counted.

This post shows how that server is built, in plain terms, and one design choice that came from imagining the worst possible moment: 6 AM, a ringing phone, and a slow database.

## The shape of the system

Ryup's backend is a single program written in **Go**, a language known for fast, simple servers. The pieces are:

- **Caddy** is the front door. It handles HTTPS (the secure connection) so the Go program does not have to.
- **Gin** is a Go web framework. It turns incoming requests such as "give me my profile" into calls to our own code.
- **Postgres** is the database. It stores users, alarms, scores and streaks.
- **Object storage** holds voice recordings, in a store that speaks the same protocol as Amazon S3.
- A **speech-to-text** service turns the recording into written words.
- An **AI model** reads the words and scores how well you did the activity.
- **Scheduled jobs** run in the same program: reminders, streak checks and cleanup.

The phone never talks to those last four directly. Everything goes through our API, which keeps the secret keys off the phone.

## Who are you? Sign-in without storing passwords

People sign in with Google (and, on iPhone, with Apple). We use **Firebase Authentication** for that. The phone gets a signed token that says who it is, and sends the token with every request. The Go server checks the signature and trusts the answer. We never see or store a password.

The server then knows your account, and everything else, such as your plan or your morning, is looked up from our own database.

## A morning, step by step

1. The alarm rings and you start the activity.
2. You read a passage and answer a question. The phone records your voice and uploads it.
3. The server stores the clip, sends it to the speech-to-text service, and sends the words to the AI scorer.
4. The result comes back as a score. The server saves it and updates your streak.
5. The app shows your results.

One rule we are careful about: a morning counts only when your alarm falls in a set early-morning window. An alarm outside it still works, but the app tells you plainly that it will not count toward your streak, instead of pretending.

## Your voice is deleted after seven days

A recording of someone's voice is sensitive. So recordings are deleted automatically seven days after upload, by a scheduled job, and the same cleanup runs when an account is deleted. We also tell people this in the app's privacy policy, and in our store submissions, which must match what the server really does.

## Small jobs that run on their own

Not everything is triggered by a tap. The same Go program runs scheduled jobs on a timer: clearing old data, sending a streak reminder, and checking sessions that never finished. Each job records when it last succeeded and when it last failed, so one broken job is visible instead of failing silently.

## Faster by doing two things at once

The app asks for your profile every time it opens. Building that answer needs two separate lookups, one for your plan and one for your streak. Instead of waiting for one and then the other, the server runs them at the same time and waits for the slower of the two. It is a small change, but it runs on every launch, so it adds up.

## The 6 AM rule: answer fast, even when you are saying no

Here is the scenario we designed for. The database does not go down. It gets slow: a failover, a noisy neighbour on shared hardware. It still accepts connections, but every request takes a long time. Each waiting request holds a database connection, so more and more requests pile up.

We already stop requests from waiting forever with a timeout. But fifteen seconds is a long time to stare at a spinner while your alarm is ringing, and the final answer would be a vague error.

So the server has a **load limit**. Once more than a set number of requests are in progress, new ones are refused immediately with a clear "server busy, try again in a second" answer. The app can act on that, and the person gets an honest answer in a fraction of a second. This only applies to the real API, never to the health checks, because a health check that gets refused makes the load balancer think the server is dead and stop sending traffic. That would turn a slow morning into an outage.

## Things we learned

- Design for slow, not only for down. A slow dependency causes more outages than a dead one.
- Put one clear rule in one place. Our "what plan do you have?" logic lives in one function, and every screen asks it.
- Run background jobs in the same program until you truly need to split them. Fewer moving parts are easier to run.
- Say what you delete, then really delete it. Privacy is a promise that code has to keep.

The server runs in a container and ships through an automatic pipeline, which we describe in [the hosting post](/blog/deploy-go-backend-aws-docker-github-actions). And the part that tells the server about subscription purchases is in [the billing post](/blog/flutter-subscriptions-revenuecat-app-store-google-play).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)
author: Softogram
coverAlt: Diagram: the Ryup app calls a Caddy HTTPS front door, then a Go API built with Gin, which uses Postgres, object storage for voice clips, a speech-to-text service and an AI scorer; scheduled jobs run alongside.

title: Deploy a Go backend with Docker, AWS and GitHub Actions
excerpt: How we ship Ryup's backend: commit-tagged images, AWS registry, deploys with no SSH or stored keys, smoke tests, instant rollback and a stalled release.
content:
Writing the code is half the job. The other half is getting it onto a server in a way that is boring, repeatable and easy to undo. For Ryup, "boring" is the goal. A deploy that makes anyone nervous is a deploy that will be done too rarely, and then done badly.

This post follows one change from a merge on GitHub to a live server, and explains the choices that make it safe.

## The big picture

When code is merged into the `main` branch, an automated pipeline builds it, stores it, and runs it on our server. Here is each step in plain terms:

1. **GitHub Actions** is GitHub's automation. It runs our checks first: formatting, tests, the whole suite.
2. It builds a **Docker image**, which is a sealed package of our program and everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on any machine.
3. The image is **tagged with the exact commit ID** and pushed to **AWS's container registry** (a storage place for images).
4. A deploy command tells the server to pull that image and restart.
5. The server checks its own health, and then we run **smoke tests** against the live address.

The server itself is a small machine in an AWS region in Mumbai. It runs our Go program and Caddy (the HTTPS front door) together with Docker Compose, a tool that starts several containers as one set.

## Tag by commit, never "latest"

A tag is a label on an image. The lazy label is `latest`. We refuse it. A label that keeps moving cannot be rolled back to, and it cannot answer the question "what is actually running right now?"

Instead, every image is tagged with its commit ID. If production misbehaves, you can say exactly which code it is running, down to the line. Our registry is also set so that a tag, once pushed, **cannot be overwritten**. A tag always means one build.

## Rolling back takes seconds

Because every old image still exists, a rollback is the same deploy command with an older tag. There is no rebuild. At seven in the morning, with something broken, "type one command and wait a few seconds" is exactly what you want.

## No SSH keys, no passwords stored anywhere

Most guides tell you to put an SSH key or a cloud access key into your CI settings. We avoid both. Anything stored there never expires, and whoever finds it can use it.

Instead:

- GitHub proves **who it is** to AWS with a short-lived signed token, and AWS hands back temporary credentials that last minutes. This is called OIDC. There is no long-lived AWS key in the repository.
- The deploy command goes to the server through **AWS Systems Manager**, a managed channel, so the server does not even need an open SSH port.

The result is that a stolen GitHub login yields nothing durable. We used the same idea for the Android store upload: Google Play publishing works through keyless sign-in, because our cloud organisation blocks creating long-lived service account keys by default. That default turned out to be exactly right.

## "Running" is not "working"

After a deploy, the pipeline does not just print success. It does two checks:

- **A readiness check** asks the app, inside the server, "can you reach your database?" It must answer within sixty seconds, because a container that started but cannot talk to Postgres is not a working release.
- **Smoke tests** then ask from the outside, using the real public address, "can a person actually have a morning?" They check the database schema the code expects, the reference data, the content library, and that voice recordings get deleted. Because they use the public address, the front door, TLS and DNS are part of the answer, not hidden assumptions.

If a smoke test fails for a known, written-down reason, it goes on a list with a date and an issue number. Nothing is silenced quietly.

## The release that stalled, and what fixed it

Here is the honest part. After we merged the subscription work, nothing reached production. The release runs only when we merge to `main` on purpose, and it showed a failure within one second, with no steps ever run.

That pattern means one thing for us: the account that pays for GitHub's build minutes had a problem. Our team's billing had lapsed, and GitHub refused to start any job at all. It looks like a broken pipeline, but it is only a bill. After we fixed the payment, we re-ran the release and it failed again, this time with a clear message: the image with that commit's tag already existed, and the registry would not let us overwrite it.

That message was actually good news. The image had been built and pushed before the failure. It only had never been deployed. So we ran the same workflow with that tag supplied by hand. Providing a tag tells the pipeline to skip the build and only deploy, and it finished in under thirty seconds.

Two lessons from this:

- A "failed" pipeline can be a billing problem. Check that before reading code.
- Immutable tags protect you from yourself. The error that annoyed us was the system doing its job.

## Why releases are manual on purpose

We learned that build minutes cost money, and a team can burn a month's allowance in a week if every pull request triggers a full run. So day-to-day work costs nothing on GitHub: we run the same checks locally before merging. The hosted pipeline spends minutes only on a deliberate release. That also means "accidentally shipped to production" is not a thing we need to design against.

## What we would tell another team

- Tag every image with the commit. Refuse `latest`.
- Make rollback the same command as deploy, with an older tag.
- Keep long-lived keys out of CI, and use short-lived credentials.
- Test the real public address after every deploy, not only the container.
- When a pipeline fails instantly with no steps, check billing first.

You can read what the server does once it is running in [the backend post](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app), and how the app is built in [the Flutter post](/blog/flutter-app-architecture-riverpod-ios-android).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)

title: Flutter subscriptions with RevenueCat: what went wrong
excerpt: How we added subscriptions to Ryup with RevenueCat, a signed webhook and a Go backend, and the App Store and Google Play setup mistakes that cost us days.
content:
Selling a subscription sounds like one feature. In practice it is a chain of five systems that all have to agree: your app, Apple or Google, a billing service, your backend and your database. If any link is wrong, a person pays and gets nothing, or gets the plan without paying.

Ryup's first version shipped free, on purpose. Billing was the next big piece. This post is about how we built it, and an honest list of what went wrong, because the mistakes are the useful part. At the time of writing, Android is configured and the iPhone side is waiting on Apple, so this is a story in progress.

## Why we used RevenueCat

Apple and Google each have their own purchase system, with different rules, different receipts and different words for the same things. You could build both yourself. You would then maintain two integrations forever.

**RevenueCat** sits in the middle. The app talks to one SDK (a code library), RevenueCat talks to both stores, and your backend hears about every purchase through one **webhook**. A webhook is a web address on your server that another service calls to say "something happened". One system to learn, instead of two.

## The path of a purchase

1. The person taps **Choose this plan** in the app.
2. The store's own purchase sheet appears. The store, not our app, takes the payment.
3. The store tells RevenueCat.
4. RevenueCat sends a message to our backend: a signed webhook.
5. The backend saves the plan against that person's account.
6. The app asks the backend, "what plan do I have?" and shows the answer.

Notice who owns the truth: **our backend decides what plan you have**, not the phone. The phone can be wrong, offline or tampered with. The database cannot.

## Two details that make it safe

**1. Who is buying?** RevenueCat does not know your users. By default it invents an anonymous ID, and then a webhook arrives for a person your backend has never heard of. So the app tells RevenueCat the real Ryup account ID right after sign-in. Now the webhook carries an ID our backend recognises. A webhook for an unknown account is logged and ignored, not crashed on.

**2. Is this message real?** Anyone could call your webhook address and say "grant this person a plan". So each message is **signed**: it carries a code that only RevenueCat and our server can produce, using a shared secret. The server checks it first. An unsigned or wrongly signed request is refused. When we left the secret out of a server's settings, the address answered "not found" instead of "refused", which turned out to be a handy way to tell whether the feature was switched on.

Our server also stores each webhook event by its unique ID, so if RevenueCat sends the same event twice, it is recorded once.

## A switch that must be flipped on purpose

The app has a billing mode: `mock` or `real`. Mock pretends purchases work, for development. Real talks to the stores. The default is mock, which is dangerous in one specific way: if someone forgets to set it, the app quietly uses fake billing and nobody is ever charged. So a test reads our real config files and fails if any build does not state its mode out loud, and production is the only one allowed to be real. Changing it takes a deliberate edit.

## What went wrong

**The test store wanted a price we could not set.** RevenueCat has a fake test store, so you can try purchases without real money. We created our test product through RevenueCat's API, and the app showed "something went wrong". What fixed it: RevenueCat's API had no field for setting a price on a test product, and the app could not load a product that had none. We created the product in the dashboard instead, where price is a required step, and it loaded. Lesson: when an API and a dashboard disagree, the dashboard is usually the one doing the full job.

**The real store product sat in "missing metadata".** After setting up the real App Store product, the app still failed. We asked Apple's own API for the subscription's state, and it said exactly what was wrong: `MISSING_METADATA`. Two things were never filled in, a review screenshot of the purchase screen and a display name for the subscription group. Once both were added, the state became `READY_TO_SUBMIT`. Lesson: ask the lowest layer. A document, a dashboard and a console can each say "done" while the API underneath says otherwise.

**One agreement that no code can replace.** Apple requires a signed Paid Apps Agreement, with bank and tax details, before real subscriptions can work, and as far as we can tell before the app can even load the product in sandbox testing. It is a legal form, not an engineering task, and it can take days. Plan for it at the very start, not at the end.

**Bundle IDs decide everything.** Apple matches a purchase to the app's exact bundle ID. Our test and staging builds have different IDs, so they cannot use the real subscription. Real billing can only be tested with the production app ID, signed in with a **sandbox tester**, a special fake account that Apple lets you create so purchases cost nothing. The same idea exists on Google Play as "license testing".

**Test periods are short on purpose.** Sandbox subscriptions renew every few minutes, to let you see renewals without waiting a month. That is helpful, but it also means a plan can appear to switch off between two requests. When we saw "no plan" right after a purchase, it was a few-minute gap between two renewals, not a bug.

## What we would tell another team

- Let your own backend decide the plan. Never trust the phone.
- Pass your real user ID to the billing service at sign-in.
- Sign and verify every webhook, and store each event ID once.
- Start the store paperwork first. It is the slowest part.
- When something fails, ask each layer directly (the store's API, the billing service's API) before guessing.

The backend that receives those webhooks is described in [the Go backend post](/blog/go-backend-gin-postgres-for-a-mobile-app), and the Flutter structure that keeps billing separate from screens is in [the architecture post](/blog/flutter-app-architecture-riverpod-ios-android).

**Try Ryup:** [Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.softogram.ryup_app)
